name: Aoki Lock to Crucifix
description: A crucifix traps one opposing arm with the legs and the other with the arms. An Aoki foot capture needs a separate positional change before either arm trap.
summary: A crucifix controls one opposing arm with the legs and the other with the arms; an Aoki foot capture does not supply either arm trap.
overview:
The initial Aoki Lock Control configuration must be identified before considering Crucifix. The captured limb is the foot and lower leg. This is distinct from an omoplata-style shoulder trap and from a bent-knee calf slicer. Either player can become the foot-lock attacker during an entanglement exchange. The reviewed instruction does not establish a direct Aoki Lock Control-to-Crucifix connection. Release the original lock safely and establish the destination's own prerequisites; do not treat these checkpoints as a demonstrated continuous entry.

The opposing foot is turned outward and enclosed near the armpit, upper arm, and forearm. Rotational foot locks can injure the ankle or knee before pain provides useful warning. Use cooperative capture-and-release practice, no spinning escapes, and the event's actual division rules. Open the original connection before either partner turns, rises or changes the captured limb.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting and Rob Biernacki — the Aoki lock](https://www.grapplearts.com/the-step-by-step-aoki-lock/); [IBJJF — current rule resources](https://ibjjf.com/books-videos).

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): Which limb is controlled before any new arm traps?
flashcards.answer: The opposing foot is turned outward and enclosed near the armpit, upper arm, and forearm.
flashcards.answer_line: The outward-turned foot and lower leg

plausible: A straight foot aligned with the forearm
An inward-turned foot beside the ribs
trap: The calf alone with the heel left outside

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): Why can a small bridge load the initial capture?
flashcards.answer: The upper-body enclosure fixes the outward-turned foot while the leg connection restrains the hip, so even a small bridge can create rotational load. Rotational foot locks can injure the ankle or knee before pain provides useful warning. Use cooperative capture-and-release practice, no spinning escapes, and the event's actual division rules.
flashcards.answer_line: The enclosed foot rotates against the restrained hip

plausible: The knee straightens over a fulcrum at your hip
The bent calf compresses around a knee-fold fulcrum
trap: The foot extends in a straight line without rotation

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): Before reallocating your legs to an arm trap, what releases?
flashcards.answer: Open the original connection before either partner turns, rises or changes the captured limb.
flashcards.answer_line: The original foot and hip controls

plausible: Only the hand clasp while the instep stays wedged
Only the hip frame while the heel stays enclosed
trap: Only the heel support while the instep stays pinned

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): Where must you gain access to build the crucifix separately?
flashcards.answer: Obtain a separate position behind or beside the shoulders with both arms accessible.
flashcards.answer_line: Behind or beside the shoulders, with both arms accessible

plausible: In front of the hips, retaining the lower-leg enclosure
Beside the near knee while the opponent keeps both elbows inside
trap: Facing the chest with only the near wrist available

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): How are the two opposing arms divided in crucifix control?
flashcards.answer: One arm must be contained by the legs and the other by an upper-body connection.
flashcards.answer_line: One held by your legs, the other by your arms

plausible: Both held by your legs with your arms free
One wrist held while the other arm stays free
trap: A leg-held arm with the other elbow free

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): Both arms are held. How can a training partner signal stop?
flashcards.answer: Stabilize the crucifix while keeping both shoulders comfortable and an agreed verbal tap available.

plausible: Keep trying to reach the mat with a trapped hand
Wait for the holder to notice a change in breathing
trap: Wait for an arm to slip free before calling stop

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): What keeps the captured leg from freely following the foot?
flashcards.answer: The initial Aoki enclosure works with a leg/hip connection; no crucifix arm control exists yet.
flashcards.answer_line: Your leg attachment at the opponent's hip

plausible: Your arm grip around the ankle alone
Your crossed ankles without contact at their hip
trap: Your heel resting near the knee without a hip block

flashcards.answer: The captured limb is the foot and lower leg. This is distinct from an omoplata-style shoulder trap and from a bent-knee calf slicer. Release the original lock safely and establish the destination's own prerequisites; do not treat these checkpoints as a demonstrated continuous entry.

plausible: Only the leg-held arm; the foot grip controls the other
Only the upper-body arm trap; the hip clamp traps an arm
trap: Only tighter leg pressure; both arms are already captured

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): An arm stays fixed during repositioning. What must change?
flashcards.answer: Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.
flashcards.answer_line: Open that arm restraint before changing direction

plausible: Release the hand clasp but leave the arm wedged
Move the shoulders first and release the arm afterward
trap: Rotate the hips while keeping the shoulder stationary

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (attacker): In the initial foot capture, where does the instep sit?
flashcards.answer: Recognize the instep-under-upper-arm relationship without applying rotational finishing pressure.
flashcards.answer_line: Under the upper arm beside the armpit

plausible: Above the upper arm with the heel under the armpit
In the elbow fold with the armpit left open
trap: Between the palms with no upper-arm contact

defender.description: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (defender): Keep the shoulders facing the opponent before a seatbelt closes. Hand fight any arm approaching the neck while maintaining a stable base.
defender.overview:
The initial Aoki Lock Control configuration must be identified before considering Crucifix. The captured limb is the foot and lower leg. This is distinct from an omoplata-style shoulder trap and from a bent-knee calf slicer. Either player can become the foot-lock attacker during an entanglement exchange. The reviewed instruction does not establish a direct Aoki Lock Control-to-Crucifix connection. Release the original lock safely and establish the destination's own prerequisites; do not treat these checkpoints as a demonstrated continuous entry.

Keep the shoulders facing the opponent before a seatbelt closes. Hand fight any arm approaching the neck while maintaining a stable base. Avoid exposing an isolated arm while turning to face the opponent.

Insert elbows and knees when space opens after the original control is released. Wait for a trapped foot or arm to be released before changing direction. Tap before pressure develops rather than completing a positional escape through a lock.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Once the foot is released, keep each elbow close to the torso while facing the opponent. This prevents an isolated arm becoming accessible to the separate crucifix entry, without promising a turtle turn from the old leg capture.

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (defender): After the foot is free, what denies access behind your shoulders?
flashcards.answer: Keep the shoulders facing the opponent before a seatbelt closes.
flashcards.answer_line: Turn to face the opponent with elbows close

plausible: Turn your hips while leaving your shoulders exposed
Face the opponent with both elbows reaching wide
trap: Keep shoulders turned away while tucking both elbows

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (defender): After release, which hand-fight takes priority near your neck?
flashcards.answer: Hand fight any arm approaching the neck while maintaining a stable base.
flashcards.answer_line: Catch the arm coming over your shoulder

plausible: Hold the wrist below your far armpit first
Press the opponent's upper arm toward your chest
trap: Use both hands to push the hip-side knee away

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (defender): What early arm position makes a leg trap harder to acquire?
flashcards.answer: Keep the elbow connected before the opponent's legs isolate the arm; do not wrench out of a secured trap.

plausible: Arm posted long behind your hip
Wrist reaching across both opposing knees
trap: Both arms extended so the opponent must choose

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (defender): After release, how can your knee help block the new entry?
flashcards.answer: Insert elbows and knees when space opens after the original control is released.
flashcards.answer_line: Return it inside beside the near elbow

plausible: Point it away while reaching with a straight arm
Keep it outside the opponent's hip as your elbow returns
trap: Bring it inside while lifting the elbow off your ribs

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock to Crucifix (defender): Why is rolling unsafe while an old foot or new arm trap is fixed?
flashcards.answer: Wait for a trapped foot or arm to be released before changing direction.
flashcards.answer_line: The torso can turn against an immobilized joint

plausible: The grips open before the torso has rotated far enough to load them
The fixed joint follows the shoulder line through the turn
trap: The direction of the landing matters more than the retained restraint
